docs.title: Hands on with OpenTelemetry Weaver
docs.text:
Weaver is a way to ensure your telemetry "looks right" and to give developers, SREs and teams a common language and set of tooling to make this easy enterprise-wide.

In this demo we imagine that we work for the ACME Corporation and we want to define a new standard attribute across our organisation to represent a cost code. Our organisation mandates that this cost code be present on every telemetry record so that we can efficiently cross charge storage costs by cost centre. Furthermore, our organisation mandates that every cost code has the syntax: [UPPERCASE_ALPHA]{3}[NUMBERS][4] for example: ABC1234.

That's easy to say, harder to do in a large enterprise:

  • How does ACME Corp define this rule in a place that everyone can access? Word of mouth? A word doc on Sharepoint? A company wide email?
  • How does ACME Corp make it easier for teams to adopt this standard?
  • How does ACME Corp make it easy for teams to "self-audit" to ensure their own telemetry is in compliance with the org policy?
  • How does ACME Corp ensure that standards don't slip after a while?

The answer is to define a standard convention that the entire company agrees upon in an easily digestible format and provide tooling so teams can audit their own telemetry to ensure they're up to standard.

This is what the OpenTelemetry Weaver project offers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You'll need Python and Docker installed (or equivalent so you can run docker ps).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
Part 1: the basics

  1. Get started: clone the repo and run Weaver against a small Python script that emits 3 log records
  2. Interpret the output: understand what Weaver tells you
  3. How it works: see how the conventions and policy are defined

Part 2: a realistic example

  1. Checking log files: check plain-text log lines with an OpenTelemetry Collector, then fix the Collector config until Weaver is happy

docs.title: Get Started (Part 1)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/agardnerIT/otel-weaver-hands-on
cd otel-weaver-hands-on

# Create a Python virtual environment and install dependencies for later
python -m venv .
source bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Pull down the weaver image
docker pull otel/weaver

# Validate the file syntax (should be OK on a fresh clone)
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/work -w /work otel/weaver registry check -r /work/model

Now open 2 terminal windows:

  • Terminal 1 will be running weaver in live-check mode. This is a server that accepts incoming telemetry and checks that telemetry against your conventions. After a certain (configurable) amount of time, the process will end (you can also press Ctrl+C to prematurely stop it) and a report will be generated.
  • Terminal 2 will be used to send demo telemetry to weaver. In this demo we send 3 log lines, each carrying its own cost code attribute.

docs.title: Terminal 1
docs.text:
Will run for 30s or until you press Ctrl+C:

docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/work -w /work -p 4317:4317 -p 4320:4320 otel/weaver registry live-check -r /work/model --advice-policies /work/policies --otlp-grpc-address 0.0.0.0 --inactivity-timeout 30

docs.title: Terminal 2
docs.text:
This Python file will send 3 log records to Weaver then exit.

python emit_test_logs.py

You will see:

=== Sending: good log with attributes: {'service.name': 'team-a', 'acme.cost.code': 'ABC1234'} to Weaver ===
=== Sending: bad-format log with attributes: {'service.name': 'team-b', 'acme.cost.code': 'abc-12'} to Weaver ===
=== Sending: wrong-key log with attributes: {'service.name': 'team-c', 'cost-code': 'ABC1234'} to Weaver ===

When the script is finished, you can switch to Terminal 1 and press Ctrl+C to stop Weaver.

Next: interpret the output. Once you're comfortable, move on to Part 2: checking log files.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The story starts with the model/manifest.yaml file. This file says "we're defining a new schema called acme and also importing another pre-existing schema from the OpenTelemetry project."

model/manifest.yaml pairs with model/imports.yaml and this file just tells weaver to import everything from the dependencies (i.e. the pre-existing OTEL semantic conventions).

docs.title: The attribute key
docs.text: Now our custom part. In model/cost.yaml we define a brand-new, never-before-seen attribute called acme.cost.code inside its own attribute group and we give some human readable descriptions. Importantly these examples and descriptions are NOT what weaver looks at to decide whether live telemetry is "correct" or not. This is PURE human readable metadata.

docs.title: The valid value
docs.text:
We have the key defined as acme.cost.code but how do we tell Weaver the valid value syntax? We do so in policies/cost_code.rego. This .rego file (pronounced RAY-GO) checks every piece of incoming telemetry and if lines 6-9 ALL MATCH then the rule fires:

  1. The input is an attribute
  2. The attribute has a name (key) of acme.cost.code
  3. The value of acme.cost.code is a string
  4. The value does NOT match the regex ^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}$ (for example ABC1234)

If those 4 things are true, a result is sent back to weaver:

{
  "id": "invalid_cost_code",
  "level": "violation",
  "context": { "<attribute-name>": "<attribute-value>" },
  "message": "acme.cost.code value <attribute-value> does not match ^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}$"
}

docs.title: Required attribute (Part 2)
docs.text: The same file has a second rule, missing_cost_code, which fires when a log record has no acme.cost.code attribute at all. This is also what flags the cost-code record in Part 1, and it rejects the unparsed log line in Part 2: a log body with cost.code=ABC12345 inside it is just text, not an attribute.

docs.title: Interpreting output
docs.text:
Weaver offers JSON and YAML output but by default we use the terminal output as it's more human-friendly.

In Terminal 1 you should see 3 repeated output blocks of Resource, Instrumentation scope and Log - one per log line.

Focus on the Log output. That's where the acme.cost.code attribute lives. (The Resource blocks only differ by service.name and carry one improvement each, because the OpenTelemetry-added service.instance.id attribute isn't stable yet. That's fine, we should be aware of it, but it's nothing serious.)

docs.title: Record 1: compliant
docs.text:
Instrumentation scope good

Log
    acme.cost.code = ABC1234
    code.file.path = /path/to/emit_test_logs.py
    code.function.name = <module>
    code.line.number = 28

Every attribute is green. The key exists and the value matches the cost code format.

docs.title: Record 2: invalid value
docs.text:
The second block has a more serious warning - a violation - and it's telling us that the value for acme.cost.code doesn't match the regex rule.

Instrumentation scope bad-format

Log
    acme.cost.code = abc-12
        - [violation] acme.cost.code value 'abc-12' does not match ^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}$
    code.file.path = /path/to/emit_test_logs.py
    code.function.name = <module>
    code.line.number = 28

docs.title: Record 3: invalid key
docs.text:
The third Log block has two violations. The key is wrong (cost-code doesn't exist anywhere in the ACME corp schema) and, as a result, the required acme.cost.code attribute is missing altogether.

Instrumentation scope wrong-key

Log
    - [violation] Log record is missing required attribute 'acme.cost.code'
    cost-code = ABC1234
        - [violation] Attribute 'cost-code' does not exist in the registry.
    code.file.path = /path/to/emit_test_logs.py
    code.function.name = <module>
    code.line.number = 28

docs.title: Demo telemetry explained
docs.text:
• Log record 1 is COMPLIANT because it contains a log attribute with:
    • acme.cost.code = ABC1234 = Valid ACME Corp cost code key and value
  • Log record 2 is NOT COMPLIANT because it contains a log attribute with:
    • acme.cost.code = abc-12 = Valid ACME Corp cost code key but an invalid value
  • Log record 3 is NOT COMPLIANT because it contains a log attribute with:
    • cost-code = ABC1234 = Valid value but an invalid key (should be acme.cost.code not cost-code), so the required attribute is also missing

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
At the end of the output is a summary section. The telemetry received covered only 1.3% of the total available attributes (remember we're including the entire OTEL conventions too), and there were 6 pieces of advice given: 3 violations and 3 improvement suggestions, plus specifics on what that advice was.

Advisories given
  - total: 6
  - advice level:
    - improvement: 3
    - violation: 3
  - advice type:
    - invalid_cost_code: 1
    - missing_attribute: 1
    - missing_cost_code: 1
    - not_stable: 3
  - advice message:
    - Attribute 'cost-code' does not exist in the registry.: 1
    - Attribute 'service.instance.id' is not stable; stability = development.: 3
    - Log record is missing required attribute 'acme.cost.code': 1
    - acme.cost.code value 'abc-12' does not match ^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}$: 1

Registry coverage
  - total seen: 1.3%

✔ Performed live check for registry `/work/model`

docs.title: Programmatic access
docs.text: All of this data is available as JSON or YAML output by using the --output json or --output yaml flag, meaning developers and SREs can bake these tests into CI/CD processes and pipelines.

docs.title: Checking log files (Part 2)
docs.text:
In Part 1 a Python script sent perfectly structured telemetry straight to Weaver. Real applications often just write text lines to a file. This part shows how to check those.

Weaver can't read log files itself, but a Collector can: filelog receiver → otlp exporter → Weaver's OTLP listener.

In this scenario a user writes a log line to a file. Weaver rejects it because it isn't parsed into OTEL and ACME attributes. You then restart the Collector with a config that does the parsing, and Weaver accepts the next line.

Registry location

The registry (manifest.yaml, model/) lives in model/ so that Weaver doesn't try to load the Collector configs or mkdocs.yml as semantic convention files. All commands use -r /work/model.

docs.title: Terminal 1: Weaver
docs.text:
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/work -w /work -p 4317:4317 -p 4320:4320 otel/weaver registry live-check -r /work/model --advice-policies /work/policies --otlp-grpc-address 0.0.0.0 --inactivity-timeout 120

Wait for OTLP gRPC listener started. Loading the registry can take a while the first time.

docs.title: Terminal 2: Collector v1 (no parsing)
docs.text:
: > filelog/logs/app.log
docker run --rm --name col -v "$(pwd)/filelog":/cfg -v "$(pwd)/filelog/logs":/logs otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest --config /cfg/collector-v1.yaml

docs.title: Terminal 3: write a log line
docs.text:
echo 'INFO HTTP GET 200 OK /someEndpoint 201.0.100.2 cost.code=ABC12345' >> filelog/logs/app.log

The line is shipped as an unparsed body. The log record has no acme.cost.code attribute, so Weaver reports:

Log
    - [violation] Log record is missing required attribute 'acme.cost.code'
    log.file.name = app.log

docs.title: Fix it: Collector v2 (parses the line)
docs.text:
Stop the Collector in Terminal 2 (Ctrl+C) and start it with collector-v2.yaml:

docker run --rm --name col -v "$(pwd)/filelog":/cfg -v "$(pwd)/filelog/logs":/logs otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest --config /cfg/collector-v2.yaml

It uses a regex_parser to turn the line into attributes, all on the log record, just like the Python script in Part 1:

Log text Attribute Where GET http.request.method Log record 200 http.response.status_code (int) Log record /someEndpoint url.path Log record 201.0.100.2 client.address Log record cost.code=... acme.cost.code Log record

Now write a second line. Note the cost code has four digits. ABC12345 (five digits) would still violate the ^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}$ rule, so try that too once you've seen the green result.

echo 'INFO HTTP GET 200 OK /someEndpoint 201.0.100.2 cost.code=ABC1234' >> filelog/logs/app.log

Weaver now shows no violations:

Log
    log.file.name = app.log
    client.address = 201.0.100.2
    acme.cost.code = ABC1234
    http.request.method = GET
    http.response.status_code = 200
    url.path = /someEndpoint

The only advice left is an improvement that log.file.name isn't stable yet. That is informational, not a failure.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Weaver's OTLP listener doesn't accept gzip, so the Collector's exporter sets compression: none.
  • The configs use start_at: end, so only lines appended after the Collector starts are read. A restart won't re-send old lines.
  • host.docker.internal lets the Collector container reach Weaver's published port on the host.
